Slide a video horizontally across the scene while it plays:

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec, Canvas, KeyframeSpec, PositionTrack, TimingSpec

canvas = Canvas(1280, 720).video(
    "clip.mp4",
    position=(0, 200),
    width=480,
    height=270,
    fit="cover",
    duration=4.0,
    animation=AnimationSpec.timeline(
        PositionTrack(
            keyframes=[
                KeyframeSpec(time=0.0, value=(0, 0)),
                KeyframeSpec(time=4.0, value=(800, 0)),
            ]
        ),
        timing=TimingSpec(start=0.0, duration=4.0),
        easing="ease_in_out",
    ),
)

docs.title: Spring easing
docs.text:
Add natural, physics-based bounce using SpringEasing:

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec, KeyframeSpec, PositionTrack, SpringEasing

motion = AnimationSpec.timeline(
    PositionTrack(keyframes=[
        KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=(0, 0)),
        KeyframeSpec(time=1, value=(180, 0)),
    ]),
    easing=SpringEasing(stiffness=100, damping=10, mass=1),
)

docs.title: Wiggle track modifiers
docs.text:
Attach Wiggle(frequency=2, amplitude=12, seed=42) to any track to add organic, deterministic jitter:

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec, KeyframeSpec, PositionTrack, TimingSpec, Wiggle

motion = AnimationSpec.timeline(
    PositionTrack(
        keyframes=[KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=(0, 0))],
        wiggle=Wiggle(frequency=2, amplitude=12, seed=42),
    ),
    timing=TimingSpec(duration=2),
)

docs.title: Transparent video overlays
docs.text:
Export videos with transparent backgrounds (ideal for lower-thirds, animated stickers, or game overlays):

  • WebM (VP9 with alpha): VideoOptions(transparent=True)
  • ProRes 4444 MOV: canvas.export("overlay.mov", animation=VideoOptions(transparent=True))
from quickthumb import Canvas, VideoOptions

canvas = Canvas(1280, 720).shape("pill", (100, 600), 400, 80, "#42CEB7")
canvas.export("lower_third.webm", animation=VideoOptions(transparent=True))

See Transparent video for details.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Source length: If the scene is longer than the source clip, set speed below 1.0 to stretch playback smoothly.
  • Captions: Captions render above all layers in the composition to guarantee legibility.
  • Diagnostics: canvas.diagnose() automatically checks caption placement, margins, and reading speed.

docs.title: Advanced Motion & Compositing
docs.text: The sections below describe advanced animation and compositing capabilities shared across all visual layers (text, shapes, images, paths, and video).

docs.title: Curved motion paths
docs.text:
Use PositionKeyframeSpec with tangent handles to create smooth Bézier motion curves instead of straight lines:

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec, Canvas, PositionKeyframeSpec, PositionTrack, TimingSpec

canvas = Canvas(640, 360).shape(
    "pill", (60, 230), 48, 24, "#42CEB7",
    animation=AnimationSpec.timeline(
        PositionTrack(
            keyframes=[
                PositionKeyframeSpec(time=0, value=(0, 0), out_tangent=(120, -200)),
                PositionKeyframeSpec(time=4, value=(480, 0), in_tangent=(-120, -200)),
            ],
            auto_orient=True,  # Rotate layer to follow the path tangent
        ),
        timing=TimingSpec(start=0, duration=4),
        easing="linear",
    ),
)

docs.title: Handles and speed
docs.text:
• out_tangent=(dx, dy) shapes the curve leaving a keyframe.
  • in_tangent=(dx, dy) shapes the curve entering a keyframe.
  • With easing="linear", layers travel along the curve at a constant speed.

docs.title: Following the tangent
docs.text: When auto_orient=True, the layer automatically rotates to match its direction of travel (facing right is 0°, clockwise positive).

docs.title: Export support
docs.text: Curved motion paths are supported in raster animations (GIF, MP4, WebM) and HTML. Document targets (PPTX, PDF) display the initial frame.

docs.title: Transform anchors and independent scale
docs.text:
By default, layers scale and rotate around their center (anchor=(0.5, 0.5)). Customize anchor=(x, y) to set a different pivot:

  • (0, 0): Top-left
  • (0.5, 0.5): Center (default)
  • (1, 1): Bottom-right
from quickthumb import (
    AnimationSpec, Canvas, KeyframeSpec, RotationTrack, ScaleXTrack, ScaleYTrack, TimingSpec,
)

canvas = Canvas(320, 240).shape(
    "rectangle", (100, 100), 80, 40, "#42CEB7",
    anchor=(0, 1),  # Pivot around bottom-left corner
    animation=AnimationSpec.timeline(
        ScaleXTrack(keyframes=[KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=1), KeyframeSpec(time=2, value=1.5)]),
        ScaleYTrack(keyframes=[KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=1), KeyframeSpec(time=2, value=0.6)]),
        RotationTrack(keyframes=[KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=0), KeyframeSpec(time=2, value=30)]),
        timing=TimingSpec(duration=2),
    ),
)

docs.title: Export support
docs.text: Custom anchors and independent axis scaling (ScaleXTrack, ScaleYTrack) work across raster frames, GIF, MP4, WebM, and modern HTML presentations.

docs.title: Animated text and shape colors
docs.text:
Animate fills and text colors smoothly over time using ColorTrack:

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec, Canvas, ColorTrack, KeyframeSpec, TimingSpec

canvas = Canvas(640, 360).text(
    "Color in motion", position=(40, 40), size=48, color="#FF0000",
    animation=AnimationSpec.timeline(
        ColorTrack(keyframes=[
            KeyframeSpec(time=0, value="#FF0000"),
            KeyframeSpec(time=2, value="#0055FF"),
        ]),
        timing=TimingSpec(start=0, duration=2),
    ),
)

Colors interpolate smoothly in perceptually uniform Oklab color space, avoiding muddy transitions.

docs.title: Live timeline preview
docs.text:
Scrub through animations interactively in your browser without encoding a video file:

quickthumb serve scene.py --timeline

This launches a live scrubber at http://localhost:3030/timeline with frame seeking and instant reload on save.

docs.title: Parent links and null controllers
docs.text:
Link layers hierarchically using parent="parent-layer-id". When the parent moves, rotates, or scales, its children follow:

from quickthumb import Canvas

scene = (
    Canvas(320, 240)
    .null(position=(100, 50), id="controller")  # Invisible point controller
    .shape("rectangle", (10, 20), 40, 20, "#42CEB7", parent="controller")
)

docs.title: Geometry contract
docs.text:
• Child positions are relative to their parent's coordinate space.
  • Parent motion transforms (position, rotation, scale) are inherited by children.
  • Parent styling (opacity, effects, masks) is not inherited, keeping child styling independent.

docs.title: Current adapters and boundaries
docs.text: Parent links are fully supported in raster, GIF, MP4, and WebM exports. In document formats (PPTX, PDF, SVG), parented groups export as static rendered fragments.

docs.title: Text range selectors
docs.text:
Animate text word-by-word, line-by-line, or character-by-character using RangeSelector:

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec, Canvas, KeyframeSpec, PositionTrack, RangeSelector, TimingSpec

canvas = Canvas(800, 400).text(
    "Words appear one by one",
    size=48,
    color="#FFFFFF",
    position=(50, 150),
    animation=AnimationSpec.timeline(
        PositionTrack(keyframes=[
            KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=(0, 20)),
            KeyframeSpec(time=0.4, value=(0, 0)),
        ]),
        selector=RangeSelector(
            target="words",  # "words", "lines", or "characters"
            offset=[KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=-100), KeyframeSpec(time=2, value=100)],
        ),
        timing=TimingSpec(duration=2),
    ),
)

docs.title: Character ownership
docs.text: When target="characters", each glyph receives its own animation phase. Spaces and punctuation are preserved with accurate font metrics.

docs.title: Track mattes
docs.text:
Use another layer as an alpha or luma mask using mask=TrackMatte(layer="source-id"):

from quickthumb import Canvas, TrackMatte

canvas = (
    Canvas(640, 360)
    .shape("ellipse", (120, 80), 200, 200, color="#FFFFFF", id="hole")
    .image("photo.jpg", position=(0, 0), width=640, height=360, mask=TrackMatte(layer="hole"))
)
  • mode="alpha": Masks using the source layer's transparency.
  • mode="luma": Masks using the source layer's brightness.
  • invert=True: Inverts the cutout area.

docs.title: Animated shape-mask geometry
docs.text: Animate a mask's position, size, or feather dynamically using MaskPositionTrack, MaskSizeTrack, or MaskFeatherTrack.

docs.title: Native HTML shape masks
docs.text: Rectangle, pill, and ellipse masks export to clean CSS clipping in HTML slideshows.

docs.title: Owner-attached path masks
docs.text: Attach custom SVG path masks directly to any layer using LayerMask(shape="path", d="M0 0 H40 V40 H0 Z").

docs.title: Path-shaped mattes
docs.text: Reference a Canvas.path() layer as a dynamic, moving track matte for custom animated cutouts.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: Choose an image, presentation, or video to make. Each preview comes from the example linked with it; adapt its text, images, and colors for your own work.

docs.title: More ways to create
docs.text:
• Render your first cards: reuse one layout without cloning the repository.
  • AI workflow: generate, validate, and render a JSON layout.
  • Webfonts and background removal: add a typeface or cut out a portrait.

docs.title: Running the recipes
docs.text:
Most recipes use fonts and photos bundled in the repository. Install uv, then run them from a clone:

git clone https://github.com/sjquant/quickthumb
cd quickthumb
uv run python examples/instagram_news_card.py

Two of the YouTube layouts cut out a portrait with remove_background=True. They need the rembg extra, which requires Python 3.11 or later:

uv run --extra rembg python examples/youtube_reaction.py

docs.title: AI Workflow
docs.text:
An LLM is good at writing a layout as JSON and bad at guessing field names. quickthumb fits this well: the spec has a published JSON Schema, a bad spec fails with errors that point at the exact field, and a valid spec can be checked for layout problems before you render it.

The loop looks like this:

  1. Give the model the schema and describe the image you want.
  2. Load its answer with Canvas.from_json(). If it fails, send the errors back.
  3. Run diagnose(). If it finds problems, send those back too.
  4. Render.

docs.title: 1. Give the model the schema
docs.text:
Export the schema once:

python -m pip install "quickthumb[cli]"
quickthumb schema --output quickthumb.schema.json

or from Python with canvas_json_schema(). It is large (about 100 KB), so the best use is as the response schema in your provider's structured-output or tool-calling feature, where supported. Enforcement depends on the provider; validate the returned spec and review the rendered result. If you put it in the prompt instead, the layers and effects definitions are the parts that matter.

A prompt along these lines works:

Write a quickthumb canvas spec as JSON, following the attached schema.

Canvas: 1280×720 YouTube thumbnail.
- Dark navy background (#0F172A).
- Left-aligned two-line headline: "AI-GENERATED" in cyan (#22D3EE),
  "THUMBNAILS" in white, 96px, weight 900.
- Cyan outline around the canvas, 12px.

Use percentage strings like "8%" for positions. Return only the JSON.

docs.title: 2. Load it, and send back errors
docs.text:
import json
from quickthumb import Canvas, ValidationError

spec = """
{
  "kind": "canvas",
  "width": 1280,
  "height": 720,
  "layers": [
    {"type": "background", "color": "#0F172A"},
    {
      "type": "text",
      "id": "headline",
      "content": [
        {"text": "AI-GENERATED\\n", "color": "#22D3EE"},
        {"text": "THUMBNAILS", "color": "#FFFFFF"}
      ],
      "font": "Inter",
      "font_source": "google",
      "size": 96,
      "weight": 900,
      "position": ["8%", "50%"],
      "align": ["left", "middle"]
    },
    {"type": "outline", "width": 12, "color": "#22D3EE"}
  ]
}
"""

try:
    canvas = Canvas.from_json(spec)
except ValidationError as error:
    feedback = [
        f"{detail.path}: {detail.message}" + (f" ({detail.suggestion})" if detail.suggestion else "")
        for detail in error.details
    ]
    # Send `feedback` back to the model and ask for a corrected spec.
    raise

Each entry in error.details has the JSON Pointer of the field (path), the layer's id if it has one, a stable code, and sometimes a suggestion. Giving each layer an id makes the messages easier for the model to act on:

/layers/1/size (layer 'headline'): Input should be greater than 0

See Structured Errors for the full list of codes.

docs.title: 3. Check the layout
docs.text:
A spec can be valid and still look wrong: text too small to read, a word that runs off the edge, white text on a light photo. diagnose() catches these:

findings = canvas.diagnose().findings
for finding in findings:
    print(finding.severity, finding.code, finding.message)

warning low-contrast text worst-tile contrast ratio 1.04 against the layers below it is under 2.0; the text may be hard to read

Send the findings back the same way as validation errors. See Diagnostics & CLI for every check.

docs.title: 4. Render
docs.text: canvas.render("thumbnail.png")

docs.title: Asking for changes
docs.text:
Once you have a spec you like, ask for edits instead of a new design. Send the current spec and one specific change:

Here is the current spec:

<spec>

Change the outline color to #B8FF00 and the headline size to 104.
Keep everything else the same. Return only the JSON.

Small edits keep the rest of the layout stable, and a diff of the two JSON files shows exactly what the model changed.

docs.title: Why JSON rather than Python
docs.text: Models can write quickthumb Python too, but you then have to run generated code. A JSON spec is data: you can validate it, store it, diff it, and render it without executing anything the model wrote.

docs.title: Presentations and video
docs.text:
Create a thumbnail, a browser presentation, and an animated video from related layouts. The Orbit Atlas example produces these results:

Start with this small example: it renders one image, a two-slide browser presentation, and an animated GIF using the base package and built-in font. Save it as creative_starter.py and run it in the directory where you want the files; it replaces files with the same names.

"""Render an image, a two-slide presentation, and an animated GIF.

Run from any directory: python /path/to/creative_starter.py
The files are written to the current directory and replaced on subsequent runs.
"""

from quickthumb import Canvas, Deck, Fade, GifOptions


def slide(title: str, subtitle: str) -> Canvas:
    return (
        Canvas(960, 540)
        .background(color="#155BD7")
        .text(title, size=82, color="#FFFFFF", position=(64, 150), animation=Fade(duration=0.5))
        .text(subtitle, size=32, color="#D5E5FF", position=(64, 300))
    )


first = slide("Make an idea visible.", "One canvas, many possibilities.")
second = slide("Keep the story moving.", "Bring canvases together in a deck.")
deck = Deck(960, 540).slide(first).slide(second)

first.render("creative-starter.png")
deck.render("creative-starter.html")
first.render("creative-starter.gif", animation=GifOptions(fps=10, hold=1))

python -m pip install quickthumb
python creative_starter.py

Open creative-starter.png, creative-starter.html, and creative-starter.gif in the working directory. These starter outputs use a simple text layout; the previews above come from the fuller Orbit Atlas example below.

The complete examples below use the same Canvas and Deck APIs. Their scripts, fonts, images, and audio are in the repository. Install uv and clone the repository to run them:

git clone https://github.com/sjquant/quickthumb
cd quickthumb

docs.title: Cleaner Future
docs.text:
One script renders a creator thumbnail, a four-slide presentation, and a short animated video. The photographs are AI-generated; the text, shapes, layout, and animation are composed with quickthumb. The bar chart is illustrative, not real sustainability data.

uv run --no-default-groups python examples/cleaner_future.py --output-dir /tmp/cleaner-future --video

The script writes python-for-creators.png, four slide PNGs, cleaner-future.html, and brighter-planet.mp4. Existing files with those names are replaced. Video export requires FFmpeg on PATH. To also create an editable PowerPoint presentation, install the pptx extra and add --pptx:

uv run --no-default-groups --extra pptx python examples/cleaner_future.py --output-dir /tmp/cleaner-future --video --pptx

The video animates the headline and accent over a still Earth image; it has no audio. See the complete source and the export guide for format details and fallbacks.

docs.title: Orbit Atlas
docs.text:
One script renders two thumbnails, a four-slide deck, and a video with sound for a fictional mapping studio. All figures are illustrative. The bundled source images, including the people, are AI-generated; the type, shapes, and motion are quickthumb layers. The soundtrack is Fupi's CC0 "Synthwave House Loop", retimed to the film's 128 BPM. The audio source notes record the source and changes.

Your browser does not support video. Download the video. 

uv run --no-default-groups python examples/orbit_atlas.py --output-dir /tmp/orbit-atlas

The script writes orbit-thumbnail-planet.webp, orbit-thumbnail-visuals.webp, four orbit-slide-*.webp files, orbit-deck.html, orbit-film.mp4, orbit-film-poster.webp, and three orbit-film-frame-*.webp stills, replacing files with those names. Video needs FFmpeg on PATH or in QUICKTHUMB_FFMPEG; pass --stills to skip it. For PowerPoint, add --extra pptx to uv run and --pptx to the script.

Text entrances can look different in HTML and PowerPoint. Check the deck in its target app; see export details for fallbacks and the complete source to adapt the example.

docs.title: Investor deck
docs.text:
The Vela example builds ten slides with transitions and speaker notes. All company data is illustrative. It exports an interactive HTML presentation and a PowerPoint file from the same deck.

uv run --extra pptx python examples/investor_deck.py

Open examples/investor_deck.html in a browser or examples/investor_deck.pptx in PowerPoint. The script overwrites these files when run again. See the complete source and the Deck API.

PowerPoint output requires the pptx extra. Some effects or transitions may use fallbacks in a given format; consult the export guide for details.

docs.title: Product reel
docs.text:
This 35-second vertical product video combines eight scenes with animated text, charts, transitions, voiceovers, and a soundtrack. Play the actual output:

Your browser does not support video. Download the product reel. 
uv run --extra pptx python examples/product_hype_reel.py

The script writes GIF, HTML, PowerPoint, MP4, and WebM files in examples/, replacing outputs of the same name. MP4 and WebM need FFmpeg on PATH; PowerPoint needs the pptx extra. The complete source uses bundled fonts and audio. Read about video exports and animation timing to adapt it.

docs.title: Instagram Card
docs.text:
A square news card: a photo, a red label, a serif headline, and a source line.

Install uv and clone the repository to run this example:

git clone https://github.com/sjquant/quickthumb
cd quickthumb
uv run python examples/instagram_news_card.py

The script writes examples/instagram_news_card.png, replacing an existing file with that name.

docs.title: How it's built
docs.text:
• The label is text with a Background effect. Background(color="#CC0000", padding=(11, 22)) draws the red box around "BREAKING NEWS", so it grows with the text instead of being a separate shape you have to resize.
  • The headline uses a different font from the rest. font="NotoSerif" loads the serif from the bundled font folder; every other layer uses the default Roboto.
  • The red bar is a 9px-wide rectangle. It is a separate shape, so its position and height (176px) are set by hand to match the two headline lines.
  • The source line is one text layer. Two TextParts give "WORLD NEWS" and the date different colors and weights.
  • Most positions are percentages, such as ("8%", "92%"), so they scale with the canvas. The red bar is the exception: it uses pixels so it lines up exactly with the headline.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
"""
Instagram News Card Example

Creates a breaking news-style Instagram card (1080x1080) with:
- Fire background image (cover fit, darkened)
- Dark gradient overlay for text legibility
- "BREAKING NEWS" badge
- Bold headline with stroke
- Source and timestamp at the bottom
"""

import os

from quickthumb import Canvas, Filter, FitMode, LinearGradient, TextPart
from quickthumb.models import Background, Shadow, Stroke

FILE_DIR = os.path.dirname(__file__)
ASSETS_DIR = os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "..", "assets")

os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR"] = os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "fonts")
os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT"] = "Roboto"

SIZE = 1080

(
    Canvas(SIZE, SIZE)
    # 1. Background: fire image, cropped to fill the square
    .background(
        image=os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "images", "tobias-rademacher-wnF27F85ZKw-unsplash.jpg"),
        fit=FitMode.COVER,
        effects=[Filter(brightness=0.9, contrast=1.1, saturation=0.9)],
    )
    # 2. Dark gradient overlay — bottom two-thirds darkened for text legibility
    .background(
        gradient=LinearGradient(
            angle=90,
            stops=[("#00000000", 0.0), ("#000000B8", 0.42), ("#000000F2", 1.0)],
        ),
    )
    .text(
        content="LIVE  /  20:42 UTC",
        size=19,
        color="#FFFFFFAA",
        weight=700,
        letter_spacing=3,
        position=("8%", "6%"),
        align=("left", "top"),
    )
    .shape(
        shape="rectangle",
        position=("8%", "11%"),
        width=908,
        height=2,
        color="#FFFFFF44",
    )
    # 3. "BREAKING NEWS" badge near the top
    .text(
        content="BREAKING NEWS",
        size=28,
        color="#FFFFFF",
        weight=900,
        letter_spacing=4,
        position=("8%", "15%"),
        align=("left", "top"),
        effects=[
            Background(color="#CC0000", padding=(11, 22), border_radius=2),
        ],
    )
    .shape(
        shape="rectangle",
        position=("8%", 464),
        width=9,
        height=176,
        color="#E11D2E",
        border_radius=4,
    )
    # 4. Main headline — large, bold, white with shadow
    .text(
        content="Wildfires Spread\nAcross 18,000 Acres",
        font="NotoSerif",
        size=84,
        color="#FFFFFF",
        weight=900,
        position=("11%", "52%"),
        align=("left", "middle"),
        line_height=1.12,
        effects=[
            Stroke(width=1, color="#000000"),
            Shadow(offset_x=0, offset_y=6, color="#000000AA", blur_radius=10),
        ],
    )
    # 5. Source and timestamp row
    .text(
        content=[
            TextPart(text="WORLD NEWS  ", color="#FF4444", weight=700),
            TextPart(text="·  Feb 20, 2026", color="#AAAAAA", weight=400),
        ],
        size=30,
        position=("8%", "92%"),
        align=("left", "top"),
    )
    # Render
    .render(os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "instagram_news_card.png"))
)

print(f"✓ Instagram news card created: {os.path.join(FILE_DIR, 'instagram_news_card.png')}")

docs.title: Launch Announcement (Auto Layout)
docs.text:
A release card whose text has no hand-placed coordinates. The headline column and the feature row are auto-layout groups, and every color and font size comes from a theme block, so changing the copy or the brand doesn't mean re-measuring anything.

Install uv and clone the repository to run this example:

git clone https://github.com/sjquant/quickthumb
cd quickthumb
uv run --extra svg python examples/launch_announcement.py

The script writes examples/launch_announcement.png, replacing an existing file with that name.

The svg extra is needed for the sparkle, which is an SVG file.

docs.title: How it's built
docs.text:
• Theme tokens. Colors and sizes are defined once under theme and used as "$theme.colors.blue" or "$theme.sizes.title". A token that is the whole value keeps its JSON type, so "$theme.sizes.title" becomes the number 116, not a string.
  • A column group for the text. The release label, headline, and subtitle are children of one group with "direction": "column" and "gap": 22. The group is placed once, at ["7%", "44%"]; the children have no position. Add a line to the subtitle and the column re-flows around it.
  • A row group for the features. "01 GROUPS" through "04 DIAGNOSTICS" are a second group with "direction": "row", so the spacing between them stays even when you rename one.
  • Simple shapes for the art. The circle, the four bars, and the star are ordinary ellipse, rectangle, and star shapes. The sparkle is assets/images/spark.svg, turned white with Filter(saturation=0, brightness=3).
  • Checked before rendering. The script calls canvas.diagnose() and prints any findings before it renders. The same check is available from the terminal as uv run --extra cli quickthumb lint examples/launch_announcement.json.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
"""
JSON-first launch announcement card.

Exercises the quickthumb 0.5 feature set in a single themed spec:
- A top-level `theme` block with `$theme.*` token references across layers
- Auto-layout `group` layers for the headline column and feature row — no
  hand-placed coordinates inside either text group
- `star` shape primitives and decorative `svg` layers
- Film grain on the base background
- `canvas.diagnose()` before rendering, mirroring `quickthumb lint`
"""

import os

from quickthumb import Canvas

FILE_DIR = os.path.dirname(__file__)
REPO_DIR = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(FILE_DIR, ".."))
SPEC_PATH = os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "launch_announcement.json")
OUTPUT_PATH = os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "launch_announcement.png")

os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR"] = os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "assets", "fonts")
os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT"] = "Roboto"

with open(SPEC_PATH, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json_spec = f.read()

previous_cwd = os.getcwd()

try:
    # The checked-in JSON spec uses repo-relative asset paths to stay easy to read.
    os.chdir(REPO_DIR)
    canvas = Canvas.from_json(json_spec)

    findings = canvas.diagnose().findings
    for finding in findings:
        print(
            f"[{finding.severity}] layer {finding.layer_index}: {finding.code} — {finding.message}"
        )
    if not findings:
        print("✓ diagnose(): no layout or legibility issues")

    canvas.render(OUTPUT_PATH)
finally:
    os.chdir(previous_cwd)

print(f"✓ Launch announcement card created: {OUTPUT_PATH}")
print(f"  Spec source: {SPEC_PATH}")

docs.title: Podcast Promo
docs.text:
An episode card: show name, episode title, and guest, with the guest's photo filling the right side.

Install uv and clone the repository to run this example:

git clone https://github.com/sjquant/quickthumb
cd quickthumb
uv run python examples/podcast_interview_promo.py

The script writes examples/podcast_interview_promo.png, replacing an existing file with that name.

The first run needs network access to download the show-title webfont. After that it is cached.

docs.title: How it's built
docs.text:
• The portrait is the background. .background(image=..., fit=FitMode.COVER) fills the whole canvas with the photo. There is no cut-out, so there are no cut-out edges to clean up.
  • A gradient makes room for the text. A four-stop LinearGradient is solid black behind the copy and fully clear over the face. Moving the middle stops changes where the fade happens.
  • The show title uses a webfont. font=SHOW_FONT_URL points at a .ttf file on Google Fonts. weight, bold, and italic don't apply to a font URL, because the file is already one specific style.
  • One accent color. The short red rule under the show title is the only color on the card; everything else is white or grey.

docs.title: Shorts / Vertical Cover
docs.text:
A 1080×1920 cover where the whole design is a JSON file. The Python side only loads it and renders it, which is how you would use quickthumb when an LLM or a template system writes the layout.

Install uv and clone the repository to run this example:

git clone https://github.com/sjquant/quickthumb
cd quickthumb
uv run python examples/shorts_cover_agent.py

The script writes examples/shorts_cover_agent.png, replacing an existing file with that name.

docs.title: How it's built
docs.text:
• One photo, used twice. The same image appears as a wide 16:9 crop and inside the phone. "fit": "cover" crops it to each frame's shape.
  • The phone is two layers. A dark rounded rectangle is the body and the photo on top is the screen. Both have "rotation": 3, as do the three labels on the screen, so they tilt together.
  • Paths are relative to the repository root, such as assets/images/denise-jans-WIRvXd1PYlg-unsplash.jpg. The script changes into the repository root before rendering, so it runs from any directory.
  • The background has a little grain. A grain effect with a fixed seed gives the same texture on every render.

docs.text:
"""
JSON-first vertical cover example.

This script simulates the workflow where an AI agent emits a quickthumb JSON spec
and the application renders it with `Canvas.from_json(...)`.
"""

import os

from quickthumb import Canvas

FILE_DIR = os.path.dirname(__file__)
REPO_DIR = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(FILE_DIR, ".."))
SPEC_PATH = os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "shorts_cover_agent.json")
OUTPUT_PATH = os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "shorts_cover_agent.png")

os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR"] = os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "assets", "fonts")
os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT"] = "Roboto"

with open(SPEC_PATH, encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json_spec = f.read()

previous_cwd = os.getcwd()

try:
    # The checked-in JSON spec uses repo-relative asset paths to stay easy to read.
    os.chdir(REPO_DIR)
    Canvas.from_json(json_spec).render(OUTPUT_PATH)
finally:
    os.chdir(previous_cwd)

print(f"✓ JSON-first Shorts cover created: {OUTPUT_PATH}")
print(f"  Spec source: {SPEC_PATH}")

Canvas.from_json() validates the spec before drawing anything, so a malformed spec raises a ValidationError that points at the bad field. See JSON Schema & AI Workflow for every field the spec can use.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text: A text layer's font can be a family name or a URL. There are three ways to get a font that isn't installed on your machine.

docs.title: A Google Font by name
docs.text:
Set font_source="google". quickthumb downloads the family the first time, caches it, and picks the file that matches weight and italic:

from quickthumb import Canvas

canvas = Canvas(1280, 720).background(color="#0A1730").text(
    content="Hello from Inter",
    font="Inter",
    font_source="google",
    weight=800,
    size=96,
    color="#FFFFFF",
    position=("50%", "50%"),
    align="center",
)
canvas.render("inter.png")

Use this option when you want to select a Google Fonts family by name.

docs.title: A font file by URL
docs.text:
Pass the URL of a .ttf, .otf, .woff, or .woff2 file. It is downloaded once and cached:

SHOW_FONT_URL = "https://fonts.gstatic.com/s/dmserifdisplay/v17/-nFnOHM81r4j6k0gjAW3mujVU2B2K_c.ttf"

canvas.text(content="Signal to Noise", font=SHOW_FONT_URL, size=50, color="#F5F5F7")

A URL points at one specific file, so weight, bold, and italic are ignored. For a bold and a regular style, use two URLs, for example one per TextPart. The podcast promo recipe loads its show title this way.

docs.title: A local font folder
docs.text:
Point QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR at a folder of font files and refer to families by name. QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT sets the font used when a layer has no font:

import os

os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR"] = "assets/fonts"
os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT"] = "Roboto"

canvas.text(content="Hello", font="NotoSerif", weight=700, size=64, color="#FFFFFF")

All of the cookbook examples work this way, with the fonts bundled in the repository's assets/fonts folder.

docs.title: Background removal
docs.text:
remove_background=True on an image layer cuts the subject out of the photo and drops the rest:

from quickthumb import Canvas, Shadow

canvas = (
    Canvas(1280, 720)
    .background(color="#1C1C1E")
    .image(
        path="portrait.jpg",
        position=(1280, 720),
        width=620,
        height=710,
        fit="cover",
        align=("right", "bottom"),
        remove_background=True,
        effects=[Shadow(offset_x=-12, offset_y=12, color="#00000099", blur_radius=26)],
    )
)

path can also be an http(s) URL.

It needs the rembg extra, which requires Python 3.11 or later:

pip install "quickthumb[rembg]"

The first call downloads the segmentation model (about 170 MB) and caches it.

Things worth knowing:

  • The cut-out happens first. quickthumb removes the background, then resizes the result, then applies effects. A Shadow therefore follows the person's outline, not the original rectangle, and a Filter changes the colors of the cut-out but has no effect on how it was cut.
  • People work best. The model is trained mostly on portraits. A subject that stands out clearly from its background gives the cleanest edge.
  • Pin the subject to an edge. position=(1280, 720) with align=("right", "bottom") keeps the portrait in the corner whatever its size, as in the talking-head and reaction thumbnails.

docs.title: YouTube Thumbnails
docs.text:
Five 1280×720 layouts. Each image below was rendered by the script under it, which lives in the repository's examples/ folder.

To run one, install uv, clone the repository, and run the script from its root. The scripts load assets from assets/ and write PNG files in examples/, replacing existing files with the same names.

git clone https://github.com/sjquant/quickthumb
cd quickthumb
uv run python examples/youtube_thumbnail_01.py

docs.title: Before / after cards
docs.text:
A photo background, a headline on the left, and two tilted cards on the right that make the promise concrete.

  • A horizontal LinearGradient runs from almost-black to clear, so the left half is dark enough for text while the photo still shows on the right.
  • The three headline lines are one .text() layer made of TextParts with their own sizes and colors.
  • The cards are rotated rectangle shapes with a Stroke; the front card also casts a Shadow. The text on each card uses the same rotation.
examples/youtube_thumbnail_01.py 
"""
YouTube thumbnail: before / after cards.

- Photo background, darkened on the left by a horizontal gradient
- Three-line headline built from TextParts with different sizes and colors
- Two rotated cards (rectangle + stroke, plus a shadow on the front one)
"""

import os

from quickthumb import Canvas, Filter, LinearGradient, Shadow, Stroke, TextPart

FILE_DIR = os.path.dirname(__file__)
ASSETS_DIR = os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "..", "assets")

os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR"] = os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "fonts")
os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT"] = "Roboto"

# Create 16:9 YouTube thumbnail (1280x720) with method chaining
(
    Canvas.from_aspect_ratio("16:9", 1280)
    .background(
        image=os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "images", "c-g-JgDUVGAXsso-unsplash.jpg"),
        effects=[Filter(brightness=0.76, contrast=1.08, saturation=0.5)],
    )
    # Darken the left side so the headline reads over the photo
    .background(
        gradient=LinearGradient(
            angle=90,
            stops=[("#000000FA", 0.0), ("#000000D6", 0.48), ("#00000014", 1.0)],
        )
    )
    .shape(
        shape="rectangle",

        size=18,

        weight=700,
        letter_spacing=3,
        position=("10.5%", "12.5%"),
    )
    # Add headline and subtitle as rich text with different sizes and colors
    .text(
        content=[
            TextPart(text="BETTER\n", color="#F5F5F7", size=96),
            TextPart(text="THUMBNAILS.\n", color="#F5F5F7", size=78),
            TextPart(text="FASTER.", color="#0A84FF", size=96),
        ],
        size=96,
        line_height=0.98,
        position=("7%", "54%"),
        align=("left", "middle"),
        bold=True,
    )
    .shape(
        shape="rectangle",
        position=(832, 370),
        width=260,
        height=300,
        color="#242426",
        border_radius=16,
        rotation=-7,
        align=("center", "middle"),
        effects=[Stroke(width=2, color="#FFFFFF55")],
    )
    .text(
        content="BEFORE\nTOO MUCH\nNO FOCUS",
        size=22,
        color="#A1A1A6",
        weight=700,
        line_height=1.7,

docs.title: Bold question
docs.text:
A single question set very large, over a photo with most of its color removed.

  • Filter(saturation=0.32) mutes the photo so the orange accent is the only strong color.
  • Each headline line is its own text layer at a fixed pixel position, which gives exact control over the line gap.
  • The thin rule above the hook is a 1px rectangle in #FFFFFF33, white at 20% opacity.
examples/youtube_thumbnail_02.py 
"""
YouTube thumbnail: one large question.

- Desaturated photo background with an angled gradient for contrast
- Each headline line is its own text layer at a fixed position
- A 1px translucent rule above the hook line
"""

import os

from quickthumb import Canvas, Filter, FitMode, LinearGradient

FILE_DIR = os.path.dirname(__file__)
ASSETS_DIR = os.path.join(FILE_DIR, "..", "assets")

os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_FONT_DIR"] = os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "fonts")
os.environ["QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT"] = "Roboto"

# Canvas dimensions
WIDTH = 1280
HEIGHT = 720

(
    Canvas(WIDTH, HEIGHT)
    # 1. Background Image with darkening
    .background(
        image=os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "images", "denise-jans-WIRvXd1PYlg-unsplash.jpg"),
        fit=FitMode.COVER,
        effects=[Filter(brightness=0.78, contrast=1.12, saturation=0.32)],
    )
    # 2. Gradient Overlay (Dark bottom-left to transparent top-right)
    # This ensures text readability on the left side
    .background(
        gradient=LinearGradient(
            angle=110,
            stops=[("#000000F7", 0.0), ("#000000B8", 0.44), ("#00000012", 1.0)],
        ),
    )
    # 3. Typography
    # Subtitle: "ARE YOU"
    .text(
        content="ARE YOU",
        size=20,
        color="#FF9F0A",
        position=(54, 74),
        weight=700,
        letter_spacing=3,
    )
    # Headline Line 1: "BURNING"
    .text(
        content="BURNING",
        size=148,
        color="#F5F5F7",
        position=(46, 108),
        weight=800,
    )
    # Headline Line 2: "OUT?"
    .text(
        content="OUT?",
        size=148,
        color="#FF9F0A",
        position=(46, 250),
        weight=800,

docs.text: Export reference · Choose an output format

docs.title: Animated GIF & video
docs.text:
See animation timing for canonical sampling versus encoded frame counts, slide/narration clocks, captions and interactive HTML behavior.

Animated export renders per-layer animation effects and deck slide transitions as real raster frames, sampled through the same pixel pipeline as PNG output. Canvas and Deck GIF/MP4/WebM/MOV all play this animated timeline, including file exports with no explicit options.

from quickthumb import AudioTrack, Canvas, Deck, Fade, GifOptions, VideoOptions
from quickthumb.transitions import Push

canvas = Canvas(1280, 720).background(color="#101820").text(
    content="Hello", position=("50%", "50%"), size=96, color="#FFFFFF",
    animation=Fade(duration=0.6),
)
canvas.render("hello.gif")                     # defaults: 20 fps, 3s hold
canvas.render(
    "preview.gif",
    animation=GifOptions(fps=8, max_size=(540, 960), colors=128),
)
mp4 = canvas.to_mp4(fps=30, hold=2.0)          # tunable variants return bytes

other = Canvas(1280, 720).background(color="#204060")
deck = Deck(1280, 720).slide(canvas).slide(other, transition=Push(direction="left"))
gif = deck.to_gif(fps=20, hold=3.0, loop=0)
webm = deck.to_webm(fps=30, hold=3.0)

Every effect takes duration, delay, and trigger, plus two timing controls:

  • easing picks the curve the reveal follows, from the shared easing vocabulary ("linear", "ease", "ease_out_cubic", "ease_out_back", …). Legacy effects default to "ease"; canonical presets resolve their easing/feel and otherwise use "linear". A bar that reports elapsed time needs "linear" to represent its progress. HTML sends named easing and custom cubic-bezier timing functions to CSS. Named polynomial curves use the existing CSS cubic-bezier approximations: their shape is similar, but intermediate pixel states need not match canonical sampling exactly.
  • start pins the effect to an absolute time on the slide instead of chaining it to whatever ran before. Anchored effects do not move the cursor the relative effects around them are chained from, so the two styles can be mixed.
from quickthumb import Wipe

canvas.shape(
    shape="rectangle", position=(0, 700), width=1280, height=6, color="#E8A552",
    animation=Wipe(direction="right", duration=6.0, easing="linear"),
)
canvas.shape(
    shape="rectangle", position=(80, 180), width=180, height=14, color="#E8A552",
    animation=Wipe(direction="right", duration=2.4, start=0.9, easing="linear"),
)

A canonical AnimationSpec with a stagger moves each target on its own beat. Line targets are sliced out of the layer's finished render, so every line keeps the layout it was drawn with and waits off screen until its turn:

from quickthumb import AnimationSpec

canvas.text(
    content="가로로 한 번.\n세로로 한 번.\n미리보기로 또 한 번.",
    position=(80, 150), size=38, color="#F2EFE9", line_height=1.5,
    animation=AnimationSpec.rise(
        from_="bottom", distance=26, duration=0.45, stagger=0.32, target="lines"
    ),
)

Lines set tight enough to touch cannot be told apart in the render, and word and character targets have no separable band; those fall back to moving the layer as a whole.

Static text and top-level groups may also stagger as leaves of an explicit parent chain. Separated bands inherit the ancestor's full affine transform and keep their own anchors and appearance tracks. This uses the same partial band adapter and whole-block fallback described above; a staggered layer cannot itself be another layer's parent. Counter-plus-stagger and dynamic sources remain guarded. See the parent transform boundaries and runnable examples/parent_stagger.py example.

Canvas.render() and Deck.render() accept a format-specific options object for animated file output. Use GifOptions for GIF (fps, hold, matte, loop, max_size=(width, height), and colors) and VideoOptions for MP4/WebM/MOV (fps, hold, matte, soundtrack=AudioTrack(...), loop_audio, and WebM/MOV transparent=True). Both accept workers=1 and render_quality="standard". GIF sizing and palette controls are rejected for video output, and video options are rejected for GIF output. The generic render(..., quality=...) option remains reserved for JPEG and WebP raster output.

Both option models use hold=3.0 for the settled-state hold, matching hold on Canvas and Deck byte methods. It must be a finite nonnegative number; booleans and strings are rejected. A default hold is omitted from serialized options and restored when loaded; an explicit zero is retained. Narration and explicit Deck slide durations still determine the video schedule, while Deck GIF continues to ignore those per-slide durations. Deck animated video retains its existing restriction: hold=0 fails when any slide has neither narration nor an explicit positive duration, because its audio schedule requires a positive silent bed. Use a positive hold for those slides. Canvas, Deck GIF, and silent image sequences continue to permit a zero hold.

The byte methods accept the same rendering controls as keyword-only scalars: workers=1 and render_quality="standard" on Canvas GIF/MP4/WebM/MOV and Deck GIF/animated MP4/WebM/MOV, plus max_size=None and colors=None on GIF. These methods use hold and do not accept options objects. Narration uses the same Deck MP4 timeline as other video output.

File execution resolves the format before checking export policy. Canvas and Deck MP4 always play the animated timeline, with default VideoOptions() when no options are supplied. Unused authored Morph transitions do not produce fallback errors or receipt diagnostics for static files or reduced-motion execution. Reduced animation retains the encoder's holds and default transitions between slides. See animation timing for sampling rates and encoded visual frame counts and durations.

ExportResult.pixel_metrics.width and height remain the canonical first-canvas raster dimensions. They do not describe GIF resizing or MP4/WebM cropping. Image sequence results separately report their full-size output dimensions.

validate_export(target) is a declared motion-capability query, independent of file execution options. For example, validate_export("mp4") still queries animated video, even with a reduced-motion policy. Concrete svg and pdf queries describe their static document fallback with the existing raster family label. Targets are case-insensitive; jpg, jpeg, webp, png, gif, mp4, webm, mov, htm, and image_sequence are accepted as corresponding family aliases. The GIF query uses raster, while a GIF ExportResult.target remains video for compatibility.

docs.title: Narrated deck video
docs.text:
A deck can be exported as a video with a voice-over per slide:

  • Pass audio= to Deck.slide(). Without duration=, the narration duration is measured with ffprobe. An explicit duration= trims the audio or pads it with silence. A slide with no audio holds silently for hold (3 seconds).
  • deck.export("deck.mp4") and deck.render("deck.mp4") play layer animations and transitions with narration by default. deck.to_mp4(), deck.to_webm(), and deck.to_mov() return animated video bytes.
  • To show still slides with narration, author static canvases and set an explicit Cut() transition. The output is H.264/yuv420p with AAC when audio is present. Omitting a transition uses the default fade, not a cut. reduced_motion=True also selects default transitions; it is not a still-slide export mode. Existing animated layers still play in the ordinary MP4 path.
  • Add background music with animation=VideoOptions(soundtrack=AudioTrack(path="music.mp3", volume=0.16, loop=True)) on deck.export() or deck.render(). Quickthumb mixes it with the slide narration; callers do not need to pre-mix audio themselves.
from quickthumb import Canvas, Deck, VideoOptions
from quickthumb.transitions import Cut

deck = Deck(640, 360).transition(Cut())
deck.slide(Canvas(640, 360).background(color="#123456"),
           audio="voice.wav", duration=2.5)
deck.slide(Canvas(640, 360).background(color="#456789"), duration=1.0)
result = deck.export("narrated.mp4", animation=VideoOptions(fps=30))
mp4_bytes = deck.to_mp4(fps=30)

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
Video and GIF follow the HTML slideshow's timing, except that nobody can click: on_click animations play automatically, one after another, like after_previous (PowerPoint's own video export does the same). Each slide plays its transition over the previous slide's last frame, runs its animations (starting with the transition, as in HTML), then holds its settled state for the transition's advance_after if set, otherwise for hold. In narrated MP4/WebM/MOV output, the inferred or explicit narration duration (or the silent-slide default) extends the visual slide when it is longer than advance_after. A slide with no transition cross-fades in over 0.5s (slide 0 with none starts instantly); set a transition on slide 0 to animate in from the matte, which also makes looping GIFs wrap smoothly.

GIF is encoded by Pillow with per-frame durations, so no extra dependency is needed. MP4 (H.264), WebM (VP9), and MOV (ProRes 4444) require the ffmpeg binary on PATH (or pointed to by the QUICKTHUMB_FFMPEG environment variable).

Canvas MP4, WebM, and MOV output can carry a soundtrack: any audio file ffmpeg decodes (MP3, WAV, AAC, OGG, ...), encoded as AAC in MP4/MOV and Opus in WebM:

mp4 = canvas.to_mp4(soundtrack="music.mp3")                    # loops to fill the video
mp4 = canvas.to_mp4(soundtrack="jingle.wav", loop_audio=False) # plays once, then silence

The audio is always trimmed to the video length. For an AudioTrack, loop=True repeats a shorter track and loop=False plays it once before silence; loop_audio is an explicit override. Legacy string paths keep the previous looping default. GIF exports do not accept a soundtrack.

Format tips

  • Backgrounds: Frames are composited on an opaque matte (default black). Use transparent=True with WebM or MOV for alpha overlays.
  • Resolution: H.264/VP9 4:2:0 video encoding requires even pixel dimensions (e.g. 1280×720).
  • GIF Optimization: Use max_size=(w, h) and colors=128 (or 64) in GifOptions to keep GIF file sizes compact.
  • Narrated Decks: A single Deck video export supports up to 64 narrated slides. Split longer narrated presentations into separate videos.

docs.title: Canonical samples
docs.text:
sample() returns the renderer-independent reference that exports are compared against, as a JSON-serializable FrameSequence. Canvas and Deck share the same contract, and a canvas produces the same observations as a one-slide deck containing it.

still = canvas.sample()                         # settled frame(s), as PNG/PDF/PPTX draw them
timed = deck.sample(fps=10)                     # uniform grid over the whole animated timeline
probe = deck.sample([0.0, 1.25, 4.0], hold=2.0) # explicit instants, ascending
  • Frames. Each CanonicalFrame holds width * height pixels as raw 8-bit RGBA (row-major from the top-left, sRGB, straight alpha), base64-encoded in data, plus the sha256 of those bytes. index is the frame's position in the sequence and slide the page it shows. A frame whose digest or dimensions do not match its data is rejected when it is loaded.
  • Still captures (capture="still") hold one frame per page in slide order, at each page's own size, with transparency preserved. time is None, duration is 0, and timeline is empty.
  • Timeline captures (capture="timeline") observe the timeline that animated WebM/MP4 exports play: transitions, Morph, layer animations, narration-driven slide durations, and a settled hold of hold seconds (default 3) for pages without an explicit duration. Frames are ordered by ascending time in seconds, share the first slide's size, and are composited onto the opaque matte (default black), which is reported as #RRGGBB. Deck GIF export currently ignores explicit and narration slide durations, so it matches this timeline only for decks without them.
  • Sampling. fps=N (at most 120) observes every instant k / N before duration; explicit times must be ascending, and times at or past duration show the final settled frame. One capture observes at most 100,000 instants; a larger explicit list or fps grid is rejected with a ValidationError before any frame renders. This grid is an observation schedule, not an exporter's frame schedule: exporters sample each span on their own frame grid, and stretch a slide shorter than one frame to a full frame.
  • Timing. duration is the exact timeline length and never depends on fps or on the requested instants. Each TimelineSegment gives a slide's absolute start, transition_end, animation_end, and end, rounded to nanoseconds; a slide is on screen over [start, end), so a boundary instant belongs to the incoming slide.
  • Memory. A capture whose distinct frames would exceed 768 MiB of raw RGBA is rejected with a ValidationError, before any frame renders when every page of a still capture, or one frame of a timeline capture, already exceeds it; request fewer instants, a lower fps, a shorter hold, or a smaller document.
  • Environment. sample() and export() report quickthumb, Pillow and FreeType versions, the text layout engine (basic or raqm), available RAQM/HarfBuzz/FriBidi versions, and the FFmpeg version for documents with video layers. Sampling video without a working FFmpeg raises RenderingError before any frame renders. environment.fonts reports the actual font face bytes selected by that operation; the asset manifest separately describes authored references.

docs.title: Render reproducibility
docs.text:
Font family names and QUICKTHUMB_DEFAULT_FONT depend on the machine's font search path. Inspect the selected faces rather than treating those names as portable identifiers:

capture = canvas.sample()
for font in capture.environment.fonts:
    print(font.source, font.sha256, font.variations)

Each face has its resolved file path (or pillow:default), SHA-256 and applied variable coordinates keyed by the font's axis names. The hash identifies the font bytes. Pillow's embedded face reports no hash if its bytes are unavailable. Paths are diagnostic: compare hashes and coordinates across machines. Only faces loaded for the current operation are reported; unused named fonts and faces from earlier operations are excluded.

Remote and Google fonts load from content-addressed copies of their resolved bytes, so another document refreshing the original URL does not change a prefetched face. These copies live in the asset cache and follow its caller-owned cleanup lifecycle. Keep local input files unchanged during an operation.

For repeatable canonical raster output, use identical document data, input asset bytes, selected fonts and variable coordinates, rendering options and environment; seed procedural effects where supported. Different font, shaping or rasterizer versions can change layout and edge pixels. This report explains those inputs; it does not promise exact pixels across platforms or native-output viewers. Use format-specific fidelity tolerances when comparing such outputs.

docs.title: Remote assets and caching
docs.text:
render() and export() download remote images, SVGs, text fills, and fonts into a shared cache, and export() returns an asset_manifest describing every asset it used. prefetch_assets() is optional: it does the same downloads up front and returns the manifest without rendering, so you can catch network failures or stale entries before a long export, or warm the cache for offline renders. Each AssetManifestEntry has the source as written, its semantic asset_type, a status, and whatever identity it has: source_key (canonical URL), cache_key and cache_path, content_hash (SHA-256 of the bytes used), and fetched_at (UTC time of the download).

status Meaning local An existing local file. missing A local path that does not exist. network Downloaded now and written to the cache. fresh Read from a cache entry within max_age (always, when no max_age is set). stale Read from an expired cache entry, or while offline, because it could not be refreshed. stale_reason explains why. unresolved A remote reference that has not been resolved yet.

The cache is controlled by environment variables:

  • QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_CACHE_DIR: cache directory (default: the system temp directory).
  • QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_MAX_AGE: seconds after which a cached entry is refreshed from the network. When the refresh fails, the old bytes are used and reported as stale. Unset means cached entries never expire.
  • QUICKTHUMB_ASSET_OFFLINE=1: never make network requests. Cached entries are used, and expired ones are reported as stale.

docs.title: Ownership and reuse
docs.text:
Keep the same Canvas or Deck to reuse resolution across prefetch_assets(), sample(), and exports. Each canvas retains its first remote resolution result and status; a deck uses its slides' results. Remote images, text fills, and SVGs render from these retained bytes. Remote fonts, including Google fonts, load from content-addressed copies of the resolved bytes, so another document's URL refresh does not change a prefetched face. Keep those cache files available through sampling and export. Construct a new document to resolve the same reference again under the current cache policy.

PrefetchResult and asset_manifest are JSON-safe reports, not resource handles. Saving or loading their JSON does not transfer bytes or preload another document. A new document can reuse the persisted cache and reports fresh when its entry is usable. Local image, font, video, and audio paths remain caller-owned files: keep them available and unchanged through sampling or export; prefetch does not freeze or copy them. Video and audio sources are not downloaded by prefetch; remote video is read by FFmpeg when needed and is outside this cache contract. Generated content without a file/URL reference has no external asset entry.

The caller owns the cache directory and its cleanup. Quickthumb atomically writes remote cache files and metadata but does not automatically evict them. Remove unused entries only when documents and export workers are no longer using that cache; existing manifests are observations, not guarantees that their cache_path still exists. No explicit document close is required for the in-memory remote results: they are released with the document.

When neither a usable cache entry nor a network response exists, resolution raises RenderingError naming the source, the cause, and the cache directory it searched. To refuse stale inputs, check the manifest before rendering:

prefetched = canvas.prefetch_assets()
stale = [entry for entry in prefetched.asset_manifest if entry.status == "stale"]
if stale:
    raise SystemExit(f"stale assets: {[(e.source, e.stale_reason) for e in stale]}")

docs.title: Asset and plugin lifecycle fixtures
docs.text:
The shared font/texture scenarios in tests/test_asset_cache.py use a private plugin registry, a repository TTF and generated image bytes served by a temporary localhost HTTP server. They exercise public Canvas/Deck operations and cache environment settings. A controlled standard clock advances expiry without sleeping or editing cache files or metadata. No public network service or platform-specific pixel snapshot is required.

Scenario Observable evidence Regression check Network → fresh new document → expired refresh Resolution status, fetched time, changed content hashes, actual font identity and decoded PNG pixels; original documents retain their resolved bytes test_combined_resources_refresh_only_for_new_expired_documents (canvas, deck) Expired cache while offline Both resources report stale with source, hash, fetch time and offline/max-age reason before plugin execution or output; a caller proceeding gets the original RGBA/font bytes without requests test_combined_offline_stale_evidence_precedes_optional_rendering (canvas, deck) Cold offline font or plugin texture Public prefetch identifies the later slide, source URL and cache directory; plugin texture errors also identify the layer/asset path. No callback or file write occurs test_combined_cold_offline_failure_identifies_later_slide_resource (font, texture) Prefetched resources across raster and native document output Canvas/Deck raster agreement, actual font SHA, asset manifest, native SVG text and exact plugin PNG fallback test_prefetched_font_and_private_plugin_keep_shared_export_evidence Missing declared plugin dependency Escaped JSON Pointer, layer identity and prewrite failure test_plugin_declared_missing_assets_fail_before_output_or_callback Plugin native match, tolerated difference, mismatch or unsupported target Actual local SVG comparison and adopted native/PNG representation; explained fallback and strict rejection tests/test_plugin_svg.py, test_plugin_document_fallback_reports_and_preserves_output in tests/test_plugin_runtime.py Default, family, file and variable fonts Actual selected face hashes and applied coordinates in sample/export environments Font identity cases in tests/test_canonical_sampling.py

Stale refusal is a caller decision using the returned manifest, as shown above; there is no automatic refuse-stale export flag. The offline fixture verifies that evidence is available before any plugin callback or destination change, then separately verifies the caller's choice to render with those stale bytes. Cold misses fail rather than substituting a font or empty plugin texture.

Run uv run --locked pytest tests/test_asset_cache.py tests/test_plugin_runtime.py tests/test_plugin_svg.py tests/test_canonical_sampling.py --no-cov -q. These files are included in the existing automated pytest tests/ quality job. Named scenarios and parameter IDs identify the resource/document failure; expected hashes are computed from the controlled source bytes and rendered samples are compared in the same recorded font/render environment. This does not promise identical font pixels across machines or native viewers.

docs.title: SVG, HTML, PowerPoint, and PDF
docs.text: Export reference · Choose an output format

docs.title: SVG
docs.text:
svg = canvas.to_svg()
svg = canvas.to_svg(embed_fonts=True)

By default the SVG references fonts by family name (font-family="Roboto"), which keeps files small but requires the font on the viewing machine. With embed_fonts=True the used font files are inlined as @font-face data URLs so text renders identically everywhere.

Viewer support

Shadow and glow effects use SVG filters (feGaussianBlur). Browsers render them faithfully; some minimal SVG rasterizers apply filters only partially.

docs.title: HTML
docs.text:
html = canvas.to_html()
canvas.render("card.html")

The result is one self-contained HTML file. Backgrounds, shapes, outlines, and text become HTML and CSS; images and anything else without a CSS equivalent are embedded as PNG fragments. Unlike SVG, PDF, and PPTX, the page plays layer animation effects, advancing on click.

The design is a fixed-size stage that never reflows. By default (responsive=True) the whole stage scales to fit the browser window; pass responsive=False to get it at its exact pixel size. Fonts are embedded by default (embed_fonts=True), so the page looks the same on any machine.

A deck exports to an HTML slideshow the same way, with a presenter view; see Deck.

docs.title: PPTX
docs.text:
Create slides you can refine in PowerPoint or Keynote, with editable text and supported shapes. Install the pptx extra:

pip install "quickthumb[pptx]"

from quickthumb import Canvas

canvas = Canvas(640, 360).background(color="#101826").text(
    "Ready to share", font="Arial", size=36, color="#FFFFFF", position=(60, 120)
)
canvas.export("promo.pptx")

Open promo.pptx in your slide editor. A Canvas becomes one slide; use deck.export("promo.pptx") for several slides.

Editing styled content

Glow is saved as a fixed image, and outlines may use separate objects. After changing styled text or shapes, re-export from Python to keep their glow and border aligned. Some effect combinations become pictures, so the affected content cannot be edited as individual text or shapes. See PPTX compatibility for details.

Fonts and layout

Fonts are not embedded. Choose a font available both to quickthumb and in the slide editor. Font substitution, mixed-size rich text and rotation can change spacing or placement; check the result in the app you will use.

docs.title: PDF
docs.text:
PDF export needs the pdf extra:

pip install "quickthumb[pdf]"

The canvas becomes a single PDF page sized to the canvas pixels (one point per pixel). Backgrounds, outlines, shapes, and eligible text are drawn as native PDF vector primitives using the same layout math as the raster renderer. Fonts that can be safely embedded are subset when their text does not need complex shaping; unsupported text is embedded as a pixel-exact PNG fragment so its visual result remains faithful.

canvas.render("promo.pdf")
# or
with open("promo.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(canvas.to_pdf())

Fidelity

PDF shadings cannot express transparency, so translucent gradients (and gradients with translucent stops) are embedded as pictures. Blur effects (shadow, glow), strokes on shapes, and gradient/image glyph fills have no faithful PDF vector form and are likewise embedded as pixel-exact PNG fragments.

docs.title: Image sequences and render quality
docs.text: Export reference · Choose an output format

docs.title: Image sequences
docs.text:
Canvas.export_image_sequence() and the matching Deck method write the actual animated timeline as independent PNG, JPEG, or WebP files plus one manifest. The destination must be new and its parent must exist. PNG is the default.

from quickthumb import ImageSequenceOptions

options = ImageSequenceOptions(fps=24, hold=2, render_quality="high", workers=2)
result = canvas.export_image_sequence("overlay_frames", options=options)
canvas.export_image_sequence("review_frames", format="jpeg", quality=85, matte="white", options=options)
canvas.export_image_sequence("web_frames", format="webp", lossless=True, options=options)
print(result.frame_count, result.duration, result.manifest_path)

Encoding controls are keyword arguments to the method, separate from timing and compositing in ImageSequenceOptions(fps=30, hold=3, workers=1, render_quality="standard"):

Control PNG JPEG WebP format (case-insensitive) "png" (default) "jpeg" "webp" quality Rejected Integer 1–95; default 90 Integer 1–95 for lossy output; default 80 matte Rejected Opaque color string; default white Rejected lossless Rejected Rejected Boolean; default False

lossless=True and quality cannot be combined: quality names lossy compression, not lossless WebP encoder effort. Invalid types or incompatible options fail before creating output or staging. Options models contain only fps (finite, >0 and ≤120), hold (finite, nonnegative seconds), workers (strict integer 1–8), and render_quality ("standard" or "high").

PNG retains the renderer's exact 8-bit straight-alpha RGBA bytes, including hidden RGB. Lossless WebP also preserves those pixels, including hidden RGB. JPEG flattens alpha onto the resolved matte and encodes RGB; JPEG and lossy WebP can change colors and do not promise exact canonical pixels. WebP retains alpha, but fully opaque files may omit the redundant alpha plane and open as RGB in image readers. Convert those files to RGBA when consuming the manifest's logical mode: "RGBA". Authored backgrounds stay visible in every format. Odd and one-pixel dimensions retain every row and column. Differently sized slides fit the first canvas's full dimensions, with transparent padding before encoding (matte-colored padding for JPEG). Imported images are not ICC-normalized; output strips inherited profiles/metadata and makes no sRGB/color-profile claim.

The directory contains 000000.png, .jpg, or .webp, and so on, plus one compact manifest.json. It records version: "1", format: "image_sequence", document kind, encoding: "png"|"jpeg"|"webp", relative filename_pattern (%06d.png, %06d.jpg, or %06d.webp), and start_index: 0. Actual frame_count, fps, duration, width, and height describe the written files. Pixel fields describe logical decoding: PNG/WebP use mode: "RGBA" and alpha: "straight"; JPEG uses "RGB" and "none". bit_depth is 8. lossless reports the selected encoding; resolved quality and matte are recorded where applicable and otherwise null.

ImageSequenceResult adds absolute output_directory, manifest_path, and capability_report diagnostics to ImageSequenceManifest. Both models and ImageSequenceOptions support JSON round trips and model_json_schema(). They add no Canvas/Deck document fields or raster format enum values. There is no growing list of frame paths or timestamps. Repeated frames are encoded once per canonical shot and written as independent editable files, not hardlinks. Frame memory stays bounded; existing scene preparation and worker buffers still consume memory.

Timing follows animated exports, including explicit slide durations, advance_after, narration-derived visual timing, transitions, and Morph. Cumulative frame allocation avoids drift across fractional holds; short or zero-hold still slides receive at least one frame. The reported duration is exactly frame_count / fps, measured from the files actually written. This can differ from the independent timeline sampler's duration or sample count. validate_export("image_sequence") and inspect_motion(target="image_sequence") use video motion capabilities. Existing strict/reduced-motion policies and parent, Morph, caption, and worker restrictions apply.

Sequences are silent: no audio encoding, mux, soundtrack, or audio sidecars. Narration retains its existing file validation and duration inference, without the encoder's 64-audio-input limit. Image-only scenes need no FFmpeg; inferred narration lengths still require ffprobe, and video layers retain their normal probe/decode requirements.

All frames and manifest.json are rendered to an atomic staging directory before publication. The target directory must be non-existent; export fails safely if the destination directory already exists, preventing accidental overwrites.

Run examples/image_sequence_overlay.py for PNG, white-matted JPEG and lossless WebP lower-third sequences with no FFmpeg dependency. All three output directories must be fresh on every run.

docs.title: High-quality animated compositing
docs.text:
GifOptions(render_quality="high") and VideoOptions(render_quality="high") opt into a 2× layer-compositing surface followed by one LANCZOS downsample. The default is render_quality="standard", which preserves existing output. This namespaced option is separate from render(..., quality=...) for JPEG/WebP. Animated byte methods also accept the keyword-only render_quality="high" argument.

canvas.render("smooth.mp4", animation=VideoOptions(fps=30, render_quality="high"))
deck.render("smooth.gif", animation=GifOptions(fps=12, colors=64, render_quality="high"))

High mode filters prepared layers and staggered targets directly into the larger surface without retaining enlarged copies of every source image. It improves integration of rotated/downscaled edges; dimensions, timing, audio, GIF palette/size controls and workers keep their existing meanings. Frames and cached background plates contain four times as many pixels, so high mode costs more rendering time and memory. Each worker adds its own buffers, so aggregate memory can increase with worker count.

This is supersampled layer compositing, not higher-resolution source layout: fonts/assets and backdrop-dependent source surfaces are still prepared at their native size. Authored static rotation is already baked into those sources. Captions retain native rendering after the downsample, while slide transitions and keyed Morph keep their existing native-resolution paths. High mode cannot restore details absent from a prepared source and may soften very small text. See the benchmark guide for matched cost measurements and before/after text crops.

docs.title: Parallel animated rendering
docs.text:
GifOptions(workers=2) and VideoOptions(workers=2) opt into process-based frame rendering. The same keyword-only workers argument is available on animated byte methods. workers is a strict integer from 1 to 8; the default remains 1, with no automatic CPU scaling. Small/static exports may be faster with one worker because starting processes, preparing slides, and copying frames cost time. Encoding and audio mixing still run in the parent export path.

Use an importable script and Python's main guard: workers always use spawn, including on Linux, without changing the application's global start method. Interactive environments that cannot import the main module should use workers=1.

from quickthumb import Canvas, Fade, VideoOptions

def main():
    canvas = Canvas(640, 360).background(color="#123456")
    canvas.shape("rectangle", (40, 40), 200, 160, "#FF3355",
                 animation=Fade(duration=2))
    canvas.render("parallel.mp4", animation=VideoOptions(fps=30, workers=2))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Workers rebuild built-in canvases with separate fonts and video decoders. Only a bounded, ordered window of frame jobs is outstanding, preserving the existing shot durations, collapsed holds, caption boundaries, and transition order. Local video layers, captions, seeded grain and built-in motion work in parallel. Custom/plugin layers, Canvas subclasses, remote video sources and unseeded nonzero grain require workers=1. Remote images/fonts resolved by slide preparation are pinned for workers; keep local assets and font-cache files unchanged during export. A source or worker failure fails the export and preserves a pre-existing destination.

More workers require more memory: each has a Python runtime, fonts, prepared slide images and decoder caches, in addition to its in-flight RGB frame. Normal completion and errors wait for running jobs to finish and close their decoders. Pending jobs are canceled on failure; abruptly terminated workers are reported as rendering errors. An OS-level kill cannot run normal cleanup.

docs.title: Lottie animations
docs.text:
Export reference · Choose an output format

Create a logo that changes shape, an outline that draws itself, or an intro with a title and moving badge. Export a Canvas to .lot and play its vector artwork with a Lottie player, without shipping rendered video frames or viewer-side fonts.

docs.title: Create a shape-changing logo
docs.text:
from quickthumb import (
    AnimationSpec,
    Canvas,
    KeyframeSpec,
    LottieOptions,
    PathMorphTrack,
    TimingSpec,
)

square = "M20 20 H80 V80 H20 Z"
diamond = "M50 10 L90 50 L50 90 L10 50 Z"
morph = AnimationSpec.timeline(
    PathMorphTrack(keyframes=[
        KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=square),
        KeyframeSpec(time=1, value=diamond),
    ]),
    timing=TimingSpec(duration=1),
    easing="ease_in_out",
)
Canvas(120, 120).path(
    square, (10, 10), 100, 100, "#159A8C",
    view_box=(0, 0, 100, 100), animation=morph,
).export("logo.lot", animation=LottieOptions(fps=24, hold=0.5))

The square becomes a diamond over one second, then pauses for half a second. Change the two paths, color, size, or easing to make your own logo.

docs.title: Play it on the web
docs.text:
Install lottie-web@5.13.0 in your web project, add a container such as <div id="logo" style="width:120px;height:120px"></div>, and serve logo.lot from your public assets directory:

import lottie from "lottie-web";

lottie.loadAnimation({
  container: document.getElementById("logo"),
  renderer: "svg",
  loop: true,
  autoplay: true,
  path: "/logo.lot",
});

Use renderer: "svg" to keep fill, stroke, and layer opacity consistent. Canvas playback in lottie-web 5.12.2/5.13.0 has a combined-opacity defect. Preview your file in the player used by your site or app. See the developer player checks for reference versions and repeatable comparisons.

docs.title: Reuse a complete intro
docs.text:
From the repository root, generate a two-second intro with an outlined title, a self-drawing logo that becomes a circle, and a rotating badge:

pip install 'quickthumb[lottie]'
python -m examples.lottie_intro /tmp/intro.lot

The intro ends with a half-second pause. Edit the title, colors, paths, and rotation in the intro example to reuse it; the exported title needs no font files on the viewer’s device.

docs.title: Choose artwork and timing
docs.text:
Use solid backgrounds and shapes, SVG Paths with fill/stroke and holes, and position, scale, rotation, or opacity tracks. Start with the static shapes, curved Paths, or motion example.

Set LottieOptions(fps=24, hold=0.5) to sample motion at 24 fps and add a half-second final pause. The default is 30 fps; up to 120 is available for finer motion at the cost of larger files. Poses stay fixed until the next sample. The export receipt reports the resulting frame count and duration.

docs.title: Lottie path morph
docs.text:
Combine PathMorphTrack with fill, stroke, opacity, transforms, and trim. For curved artwork, adapt the logo morph example.

Keep the same contour count and open/closed states across your paths. Leave room in view_box for curves, control points, and the stroke; use uniform scaling for stroked paths. If export reports a geometry or work limit, enlarge the view box, simplify the path, or lower fps as directed. See Path morphing.

docs.title: Lottie stroke trim
docs.text:
Use TrimEndTrack to reveal an outline. This continues the logo example above:

from quickthumb import TrimEndTrack

outline = AnimationSpec.timeline(
    TrimEndTrack(keyframes=[
        KeyframeSpec(time=0, value=0),
        KeyframeSpec(time=1, value=1),
    ]),
    timing=TimingSpec(duration=1),
    easing="ease_in_out",
)
Canvas(120, 120).path(
    square, (10, 10), 100, 100, None,
    view_box=(0, 0, 100, 100), stroke="#159A8C", stroke_width=3,
    animation=outline,
).export("outline.lot", animation=LottieOptions(fps=24, hold=0.5))

Move a visible segment with TrimStartTrack and TrimOffsetTrack, or set static trim_start, trim_end, and trim_offset. Positions run from 0 to 1 over total path length in contour order, including while morphing; offsets wrap in either direction. Full 0→1 draws the whole stroke; equal endpoints and 1→0 hide it. Fill stays complete underneath. Use solid strokes and choose line_cap for cut ends. If a very short interval triggers a precision error, widen the interval. See the trim example.

docs.title: Move shapes together
docs.text: Attach Shape layers to a Null with parent to rotate or move them as a group; use the parenting example as a starting point. Children keep their drawing order and independent opacity. To fade the group, animate each visible child’s opacity. Percentage positions use Canvas dimensions. Keep animated shapes without a parent inside the Canvas at their authored pose; parented shapes can enter from outside. Parenting is available for Shape and Null layers.

docs.title: Lottie outlined text
docs.text: Install quickthumb[lottie] to add static, single-line printable ASCII titles as vector outlines. Viewers need no fonts; edit the source title and re-export to change it. Adapt the text example with a local outline font, an opaque text color, and explicit nonzero letter_spacing for multi-character text. Use layer opacity for translucency. Keep the title unrotated and without a parent. For animated or multilingual typography, choose a video output instead.

docs.title: Check compatibility before exporting
docs.text:
Call canvas.validate_export("lottie") before integrating an existing design. It lists layers and fields to change, such as gradients, images, effects, or text animation. Export also checks sampled geometry and precision before writing, so a rejected export preserves an existing destination.

For vector Lottie, use the artwork and tracks shown above. To keep raster images, effects, or other unsupported content, choose a video output; Lottie export does not silently replace them with images.

For a still version, use ExportPolicy(reduced_motion=True) with a positive hold. This exports the authored artwork rather than the animation’s final pose.

docs.title: Export methods and receipts
docs.text: Export reference · Choose an output format

docs.title: Recommended output API
docs.text:
Use export() to write a Canvas or Deck and receive an ExportResult with written_paths, capability/fallback diagnostics, pixel/timing metadata, assets and the observed rendering environment. The extension selects the format. MP4, WebM, MOV and GIF play the animated timeline. Deck video also mixes per-slide narration.

from quickthumb import VideoOptions

result = deck.export("slides.mp4", animation=VideoOptions(hold=2, render_quality="high"))
print(result.written_paths, result.fallback_diagnostics)
deck.export("slides.html")  # interactive slideshow with click-triggered motion
canvas.export("card.webp", quality=85)  # JPEG/WebP compression quality
